full_text:
The incoming 2026 NFL rookie class has been widely maligned across both [traditional scouting](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/KJZJusBVSGk) and [fantasy football perspectives](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/ryan-heaths-dynasty-rookie-rankings#/), and it had many dynasty fantasy football managers scrambling to trade this year’s rookie draft picks for 2027 selections. While that may have been a prudent move, that doesn’t mean that *every* 2026 rookie is going to be worthless. Heck, some might even be productive!

We’ve painstakingly evaluated this class through the dynasty lens, but some teams will be counting on their incoming rookies to play significant snaps as soon as this year. And for 2026, some players found softer landing spots than others.

Below are some of the *Fantasy Points* staff’s favorite rookie landing spots and their current best ball ADPs. Could any of these players end up paying off an investment in 2026?

\> The __Fantasy Points Brain Trust__ article series will recur throughout the 2026 off-season. Make sure to get all access with a [Fantasy Points subscription](https://www.fantasypoints.com/plans)!

Favorite 2026 Fantasy Football Rookie Landing Spots
---------------------------------------------------

##### __Jadarian Price__, RB, Seattle Seahawks (Round 1, Pick 32)

\> __ADP:__ Round 6, RB25 (Underdog)

I would have hated this pick if I were a Seahawks fan. But for fantasy, Price was probably the single biggest winner of the entire Draft. The combination of Round 1 draft capital and a dream landing spot in Seattle puts Price in an almost impossible-to-fail setup.

Over the last decade, Round 1 RBs have averaged 15.5 FPG as rookies (~RB12), and only two of 14 RBs (Rashaad Penny, Sony Michel) failed to clear 13.5 FPG (~RB20).

Seattle was arguably the most RB-needy team entering the Draft. At the same time, they were one of the most run-heavy offenses in football last year — their 435 backfield carries trailed only Atlanta. Granted, all those carries were divied out in a near-even split, but Kenneth Walker flashed league-winning upside when given a bell cow workload in the playoffs last year (once Zach Charbonnet went down), averaging 139.0 YFS/G and 24.5 FPG.

And I’d expect something much closer to a bell cow workload than a 50/50 split for Price in 2026. Charbonnet is coming off ACL reconstruction. He’s probably not back until the second half of the season at the earliest, and that’s [if he returns at all](https://x.com/DrJesseMorse/status/2025048106241294491?s=20). (Long term, Charbonnet is also a free agent after this season.)

Unless Emanuel Wilson, George Holani, or Kenny McIntosh scare you, it’s tough to come up with a realistic scenario where Price doesn’t finish the year as a mid-range RB2 at worst.

Currently priced as the RB25, that’s a bet I’ll take every time. *__\[Scott Barrett\]__*

__\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\___

Sometimes dreams really do come true. For those of us who hyped up Price all offseason, this landing spot and draft capital are about as good as it gets. Price steps right into the vacated Kenneth Walker role and has a chance to get off to a fast start, with Zach Charbonnet expected to miss significant time due to a torn ACL. Seattle ranked 27th in PROE last season, and despite the offensive coordinator change, not much should shift philosophically.

Emanuel Wilson and George Holani will rotate in, but Price is positioned to dominate touches. His home-run ability is a perfect fit for this offense. And for fantasy analysts and dynasty managers who were fading Price pre-draft, there’s still room to get on board. He has the profile to become a star in this offense, and his current RB25 price tag could quickly look like a massive bargain.

If you want to wait on RB2, the Price is right in the late fifth round. Enjoy his ADP while you can – it is going to trend upwards all summer. *__\[Theo Gremminger\]__*

##### __Jordyn Tyson__, WR, New Orleans Saints (Round 1, Pick 8)

__ADP:__ Round 8, WR31 (Underdog)

Chris Olave is the perfect meat shield to suppress Jordyn Tyson’s ADP much more than he suppresses Tyson’s upside in actuality. A player being “the WR1 on their own team” is one of the most historically overrated things in fantasy football; team WR2s who get drafted before the late rounds have difference-making seasons at much higher rates!

 Fantasy drafters tend to overrate the importance of "being the team's WR1" within the top-100 picks. Team WR2s (by ADP) have been more likely to drastically outperform their cost. Because we (the market) are very good at identifying teams that can support multiple fantasy WRs! pic.twitter.com/QUp7SDz7Ko — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) January 19, 2026 

This is due to both a psychological bias and the fact that we’re actually quite good at identifying which offenses may support multiple fantasy-viable WRs, leading receivers from those teams to be selected in the top-100 more often. On that front, Saints HC Kellen Moore has [consistently ranked](https://x.com/SmolaDS/status/2013610924876169533?s=20) near the top of the NFL in pace (with more plays meaning more fantasy points), and his offense *just* supported two top-24 WRs by XFP/G in 2025 (17.6 for Olave, 13.4 for Rashid Shaheed) over the nine weeks they remained on the team together.

Oh, and that largely came with Spencer Rattler under center, under whom the Saints averaged 3.8 fewer points per game than with 2026 starter Tyler Shough. There’s plenty of opportunity in this offense, such that Tyson should immediately produce in fantasy commensurate with however high his talent level actually is. *__\[Ryan Heath\]__*

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Jordyn Tyson is a bit chalky given his draft capital on an ascending offense, but he has multiple paths to fantasy relevance this season and beyond. I like to look for rookies with both a path to standalone value based on opportunity and an injury path should a starter go down.

Tyson’s barrier to WR1 status is Chris Olave. Not to be dismissive of Olave, but he is coming off a career season in which he totaled 1,163 yards on 156 targets (2.09 YPRR 21st, 7.70 YPT 77th). That tells me he is a tier or two below the elite WR’s, which gives Tyson a chance to outperform his main target competition. It was not long ago that there were questions about whether Rashid Shaheed was a better receiver than Olave. On top of that, Olave has a lengthy history of concussions and will be an unrestricted free agent following the 2026 season. It is not unrealistic to think the Saints will be hesitant to shell out a big contract extension for Olave in the near future.

In terms of standalone value, there is plenty of room for Tyson to carve out a role in the case that Olave does play another full, productive season. Prior to a mid-season trade, Shaheed owned a 21.0% target share and was on pace for 124 targets across a 17-game season. Tyson’s main competition for targets behind Olave are Juwan Johnson, Devaughn Vele, and fellow rookie Bryce Lance, with Johnson being the only one to push for 100 targets in a season. While

I think projecting 124 targets would be a stretch for Tyson, but I can see him approaching the 100-target range, which would provide the standalone value that I am looking for. *__\[Bill O’Brien\]__*

##### __Germie Bernard__, WR, Pittsburgh Steelers (Round 2, Pick 47)

\> __ADP__: Round 16, WR73 (Underdog)

In Mike McCarthy’s first draft with the Steelers, Pittsburgh made it a priority to add another offensive weapon for (likely) Aaron Rodgers and whoever becomes the QB of the future. McCarthy has used 3-plus WR sets on 80% or more of dropbacks in each of his past two seasons, and he hasn’t dipped below 76% since 2021. The Steelers clearly knew they did not have enough pieces to run the offense the way McCarthy wants, so they added Michael Pittman Jr. and Germie Bernard.

Bernard is not the type of prospect anyone is pounding the table for, but he gives off long-term-pro vibes. All the reports on him basically say the same thing: he is advanced, dependable, and does everything right, even if he may never be a true standout.

Post-draft, the team talked up his versatility to play both inside and outside, which matters in an offense I expect to live in 11 personnel. With second-round rookie WRs, we mostly just want a path to playing time. And if Bernard gets on the field early, there is already a strong [trend of rookie WR production being back-](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2039473737859268795?s=20)[weighte](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2039473737859268795?s=20)[d](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2039473737859268795?s=20).

It is hard to find players going this late in best ball drafts who are projected for around 500 receiving yards and could get most of that production in the back half of the season. That makes Bernard a worthy 16th-round dart throw, even at a rising price.

Bonus points because Scott found a [dank stat](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2048140386502406353?s=20) on McCarthy slot WRs that makes the case even stronger. *__\[Zain Dhanani\]__*

##### __Antonio Williams__, WR, Washington Commanders (Round 3, Pick 71)

\> __ADP__: Round 16, WR72 (Underdog)

Antonio Williams is a somewhat uninspiring prospect in an extremely weak draft class, but his skill set and landing spot on the Commanders make him a compelling fantasy selection.

Washington lost its leading receiver in Deebo Samuel this offseason, vacating 98 targets and leaving a lucrative role wide open. The target competition that remains consists of a 30-year-old Terry McLaurin, (potentially) a 35-year-old Zach Ertz, prodigal son Dyami Brown, and a group of unproductive receivers who each failed to eclipse 250 receiving yards last season.

Enter Williams, [who ranked](https://x.com/ffdataroma/status/2044846936751288612?s=20) in the 92nd percentile in receiving yards (598) and 88th percentile in yards per team pass attempt (1.25) as a true freshman in the ACC. He dealt with injuries in 2025, but GM Adam Peters has made [his enthusiasm](https://x.com/jagibbs_23/status/2049506228166877691?s=20) for Williams’ fit in this offense clear — projecting him as the starting slot receiver with 2WR set opportunities.

At WR74, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a player with an easier path to targets in the 15th round or later — or with a comp and potential ceiling comparable to 2023 Jayden Reed (WR23). *__\[Kyle Menton\]__*

__\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\___

The 2025 Washington Commanders season was a disaster. Jayden Daniels played in just seven games, while the team fell from the NFC Championship game to a 5-12 dumpster fire just a year later. With a healthy Daniels, I believe this passing game can find itself again — in the slot.

In his 2024 rookie campaign, Daniels was top-10 in slot targets (158). Last year, he fell to 24th in his seven-game sample size per Fantasy Points Data. New OC David Blough, a former QB himself, should help Daniels find easy reads across the middle to a player like Williams.

In Daniels’ seven healthy games, he targeted Deebo Samuel and Zach Ertz on 50% of his first-reads. Both remain unsigned.

Enter Antonio Williams, who is a demon with the ball in his hands. A slot machine with little competition around him, I love Williams as a sneaky pick in 2026.

Williams has to beat out the likes of Luke McCaffrey, who ran only 39.6% of routes from the slot a year ago. This role is wide open for the taking, and a plus-athlete like Williams is exactly the type of sleeper who can help you cash in on re-draft and best ball lineups. *__\[Brian Drake\]__*

##### __Zachariah Branch__, WR, Atlanta Falcons (Round 3, Pick 79)

\> __ADP:__ Round 17, WR85 (Underdog)

Our editor [Joe Dolan](https://x.com/FG_Dolan) would probably advise against opening with two massive negatives, but eff it, we ball. The draft capital [isn’t impressive](https://x.com/NFL/status/2047859904761782492?s=20), and the nephew of Pro Football Hall of Famer Cliff Branch might just be bad at the game. Now that we’ve set a realistic baseline, let’s get to the only question that matters: what if he doesn’t suck?

Branch lands in Atlanta, competing with Jahan Dotson and Olamide Zaccheaus for snaps opposite Drake London. That’s not much of a hill to climb if the former Georgia Bulldog has any real juice. And if he does, that juice is worth the squeeze. His current ADP of WR85 is essentially free.

It may feel like a fever dream, but in 2024, Darnell Mooney posted double-digit fantasy points in eight of 16 games, with five performances of 16+ (per Fantasy Points Data). Those are legitimate week-winning spikes. He couldn’t sustain that in 2025, largely due to injuries and shaky quarterback play.

 Games with >80 receiving yards last year 1. Justin Jefferson (12) 2. Ja'Marr Chase (10) 2. Brian Thomas Jr. (10) 4. AJ Brown (8) 4. CeeDee Lamb (8) 6. Darnell Mooney (7) [ADP: Round 8] 👍 ... 16. Drake London (5) [ADP: Round 2] 👎 pic.twitter.com/hewF5RBYYz — Fantasy Points Data (@FantasyPtsData) July 22, 2025 

New head coach [Kevin Stefanski](https://x.com/Schultz_Report/status/2012717904114921913?s=20) should help stabilize things. Atlanta ranked in the bottom five in pass rate last season (55.9%), while Stefanski’s Browns finished 8th (62.2%) despite similarly terrible quarterback play.

Now enter Tua Tagovailoa. The memes continue to suppress prices, but there’s real upside if Tua gets the nod and stays on the field. The last and only time he played a full season in 2023, he supported the WR1 overall (Tyreek Hill) and the WR23 overall (Jaylen Waddle) in fantasy points per game. The number of outs with Zachariah Branch doesn’t match the price. You’re getting exposure to multiple paths hitting at once: Tua Tagovailoa outperforming expectations, Michael Penix Jr. emerging, Kevin Stefanski elevating the offense, Kyle Pitts potentially being moved, or Branch simply proving he’s a good football player.

At WR85, you don’t need all of them. You probably only need one. *__\[Good Friend Trey\]__*

##### __Kaytron Allen__, RB, Washington Commanders (Round 6, Pick 187)

\> __ADP:__ Round 16, RB59 (Underdog)

Let’s get it out of the way — yes, I am a Nittany Lion (so is Tom Brolley), so I am biased. But also understand that my brain can evaluate Penn State separately from my heart. Penn State was *putrid* to watch on offense the last couple of years, and Allen was one of the few bright spots, consistently producing despite James Franklin ceding too much work to Nicholas Singleton.

Clearly, the NFL felt Singleton was the better prospect (he was a fifth-round pick to the Titans), but I have held fast throughout the draft process that Allen is simply a better football player. Penn State’s all-time leading rusher, Allen set career highs in rushing yards (1303), touchdowns (15), and yards per carry (6.2) in his senior season, despite the team being the worst of his Penn State career and playing the fewest games (12) of his career. He’s also not a zero in the passing game, with 70 career catches and 4 receiving touchdowns.

Allen is a low-to-the-ground Weeble Wobble (his nickname is literally “Fatman”) who doesn’t have high-end speed but is hard to bring down and surprisingly elusive for his size. He has some “squint, and you can see David Montgomery” to his game, and my friend Fran Duffy from the ALLCITY Network compared him to Kyren Williams, who was also a do-it-all Day 3 pick without high-end athleticism but a superior football IQ.

The Commanders were a popular Jeremiyah Love spot in mock drafts, and the board just fell in such a way that they didn’t address RB until Day 3. Compared to some of the other Day 3 backs drafted before him, Allen landed in a pristine spot, with competition only from Rachaad White (on a cuttable deal), Bill Croskey-Merritt, Jerome Ford (also on a cuttable deal), and Jeremy McNichols.

As someone you can add with your last pick or two in best-ball drafts, Allen is an easy click, and I would not be shocked at all if we get a steady drum of camp buzz for him — not dissimilar to Bill’s in 2025. *__\[Joe Dolan\]__*

The [2026 NFL Draft](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/series/2026/nfl-draft) is officially in the books, which means it’s time to update my NFL Power Rankings since the [first edition for the 2026 season](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/betting/2026/nfl-power-rankings-post-free-agency) was released in late March. I’ve already written about the early [2026 NFL Win Totals](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/nfl-win-totals#/) before the draft, and I’ll be hitting the changing NFL Futures market and the initial rookie player props with the upcoming season coming into view.

\>Be sure to check out [Brolley’s Best Bets: 2026 NFL Futures](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/series/2026/best-bets#/) for my favorite bets all offseason…Subscribe to the Best Bets Podcast on your [favorite platform](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/podcasts/show/nfl-best-bets) and on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@FantasyPointsBetting) for year-round NFL betting talk…Join our “#official-bets” [Fantasy Points Discord](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/discord) to see our staff's wagers as soon as we make them!

My Power Rankings are designed to be a starting point for point-spread betting between two teams. I’ll update these rankings every week in my Best Bets articles once the regular season starts. I take into account recent performances, long-term injuries, coaching, and strength of schedule. These rankings are intended to help predict performances in the present, but they’re not necessarily predictive for the rest of the season. I will take my Power Rankings into account when I make my weekly against-the-spread selections in our Staff Picks articles. I’ll also consider injury reports, home-field advantage, weather, and other factors that may be relevant.

\>My top-rated team, the Los Angeles Rams (5), would be 9-point favorites on a neutral field over my worst-rated team, the Miami Dolphins (-4). Using a 1.5-point adjustment for home-field advantage ([HFA average](https://www.covers.com/nfl/home-field-advantage) was 1.4 points in 2022), the Rams would be 10.5-point favorites over the Dolphins at home and 7.5-point favorites over the Dolphins on the road.
